advances: An explicit martingale contraction reduces every one-dimensional feasible array to the two integers adjacent to its source mean without increasing mutual information. The resulting unique mutual-information minimizer simultaneously minimizes every convex target potential. Its posterior source laws are log-concave when the source is log-concave. The construction and both minima tensorize for independent coordinates. For square-law sampling this gives an exact, necessary-and-sufficient scalar test for the budget on the entire minimum-potential face. The scalar inequality and a transfer to actual mixed-integer halfspace depth are not proved here.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. Every asserted construction, minimization, and tensorization statement is proved above; exploratory numerical optimization and literature-search results are not premises.
proof:
For every feasible array, summing the row equations and using the column equations gives \(\sum_jjq_j=\mu\). Since \(\mu\in[a_0,b_0]\), its integral value or its two adjacent integers, as applicable, belong to \(D\). Its row and column totals are probability laws, so the canonical entropy definitions expand to \(I(r)=\operatorname{MI}(X;J)=S(p)-\operatorname{Ent}(X\mid J)\). We will use the finite entropy chain rule and nonnegativity of mutual information, including conditional mutual information. These follow by expanding the finite sums: mutual information is relative entropy of a joint law against the product of its marginals, and conditional mutual information is its average conditional version. Relative entropy is nonnegative, with equality precisely when the two probability laws agree, by \(\log t\le t-1\) and its strict equality condition. The same facts apply when some probabilities vanish, by restricting each calculation to its positive support.

First construct the adjacent-target channel for any finitely supported integer-valued source with mean \(k+\theta\), \(0<\theta<1\). Both sides of \(k\) have positive mass: a law entirely on one side could not have a mean strictly between \(k\) and \(k+1\). Hence \(a,b,u,v,L\) in the statement are defined, \(a+b=1\), and

\[
\theta=b(1+v)-au,\qquad 1-\theta=a(1+u)-bv.
\]

These identities give

\[
\begin{aligned}
1-\frac{\theta v}{aL}&=\frac{(1-\theta)(1+v)}{aL},\\
1-\frac{\theta(1+u)}{bL}&=\frac{(1-\theta)u}{bL}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Every probability and complement in these displays is nonnegative; thus the proposed assignments belong to \([0,1]\). The joint masses of target and source side are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &X\le k&X\ge k+1\\ \hline
J=k&(1-\theta)(1+v)/L&(1-\theta)u/L\\
J=k+1&\theta v/L&\theta(1+u)/L.
\end{array}
\]

Their row sums are \(1-\theta\) and \(\theta\). Within either source side the assignment is constant, so every positive-mass conditional source-side piece retains the corresponding one of the means \(k-u\) and \(k+1+v\). On the row at \(k\), the mean of \(X-k\) is therefore \([(1+v)(-u)+u(1+v)]/L=0\). On the row at \(k+1\), the mean of \(X-k-1\) is \([v(-u-1)+(1+u)v]/L=0\). Thus the channel is barycentric. This proof includes \(u=0\), \(v=0\), or both.

Now take any original feasible pair \((J,X)\), and apply that same construction to the integer-valued law of \(J\). Denote the new adjacent target by \(K\). Given \(J\), draw \(K\) independently of \(X\) according to the constructed channel. Then

\[
\mathbb E[X\mid K]
=\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid J,K]\mid K]
=\mathbb E[J\mid K]=K.
\]

Thus the new pair \((K,X)\) is feasible and has the required adjacent target law. The chain rule, together with conditional independence of \(X\) and \(K\) given \(J\), gives

\[
\operatorname{MI}(X;J)-\operatorname{MI}(X;K)
=\operatorname{MI}(X;J\mid K)\ge0.
\]

Moreover, equality forces \(X\) and \(J\) to be conditionally independent given \(K\). At every pair \((j,k')\) of positive joint probability, conditional independence in the construction gives \(\mathbb E[X\mid J=j,K=k']=j\), while equality in the information inequality gives the same expectation as \(\mathbb E[X\mid K=k']=k'\). Hence \(j=k'\). Consequently equality forces \(J=K\) almost surely. This proves the contraction and its equality statement directly, without invoking a convex-order existence theorem.

Consider nonintegral \(\mu\). An array supported on targets \(k,k+1\) must have their stated probabilities, because its total mass is one and its target mean is \(k+\theta\). Writing its entries as \(p_it_i\) and \(p_i(1-t_i)\) gives exactly the two linear constraints in the statement. Conversely those constraints imply the two row mean equations. In this parametrization \(H(r)=\sum_i p_i\mathsf h(t_i)\) and \(I(r)=\mathsf h(\theta)-\sum_i p_i\mathsf h(t_i)\).

The constraint set is nonempty by the explicit channel, and is a closed subset of the finite cube \([0,1]^D\), so the entropy objective attains its maximum. Binary entropy is strictly concave on \([0,1]\): on its interior its second derivative is \(-1/[t(1-t)]<0\), and continuity gives strict concavity including distinct endpoints. Since every \(p_i\) is positive, the weighted sum is strictly concave in the entire vector \(t\). The constraint set is convex, so its maximizing vector \(t^*\) is unique.

The contraction proves that no array anywhere in \(\mathcal F(p)\) has smaller information than this adjacent-target optimizer. It also proves global uniqueness. Indeed, let an arbitrary array attain the same global minimum, and contract its target as above. The contracted array has information at least the adjacent minimum and at most the original minimum, so equality holds. The equality statement forces its original target to equal its adjacent target almost surely. The original array therefore lies in the adjacent-target constraint set and must be its unique optimizer.

If \(\mu\) is integral, the constant-target array is feasible and has information zero. Information cannot be negative. If any feasible array has information zero, \(X\) and \(J\) are independent; the row identity then gives \(J=\mathbb E[X\mid J]=\mu\) almost surely. The column equations force precisely the stated constant-target array. This proves uniqueness in the integral case, including the one-site support.

Next prove the exact channel description. Suppose first that \(a_0<k\) and \(k+1<b_0\). Because the source is positive throughout its interval, the side means in the explicit channel have \(u>0\) and \(v>0\). The displayed channel probabilities and complements are then all strictly positive. Thus the adjacent-target constraint set contains a vector all of whose coordinates lie strictly between zero and one.

Its entropy maximum also has all coordinates in that open interval. To see this, if a maximizer had an endpoint coordinate, move a proportion \(\varepsilon>0\) toward the strictly interior feasible vector. At every endpoint coordinate that changes, binary entropy increases by a positive multiple of \(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)\) plus \(O(\varepsilon)\). At each coordinate already interior the change is \(O(\varepsilon)\). There are finitely many coordinates, all with positive weights, and at least one endpoint changes. For sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), the total change is therefore positive, a contradiction.

At this interior maximum, the gradient of the objective annihilates every vector in the kernel of the two constraint rows \((p_i)_i\) and \((ip_i)_i\). These rows are linearly independent since there are distinct source sites and all \(p_i>0\). Elementary finite-dimensional linear algebra therefore gives constants \(A,B\) with \(\mathsf h'(t_i^*)=A+Bi\) for every \(i\). Since \(\mathsf h'(t)=\log((1-t)/t)\), setting \(\lambda=-A\) and \(\eta=-B\) yields the stated logistic formula.

The moment constraints imply

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,t_X^*)
=\sum_i ip_it_i^*-\mu\sum_i p_it_i^*
=\theta(1-\theta)>0.
\]

For any real function \(f\) on \(D\), direct expansion gives \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,f(X))=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}p_ip_j(i-j)(f(i)-f(j))\). A constant or decreasing \(f\) has nonpositive covariance. Thus the logistic slope \(\eta\) is positive. Existence of the pair follows from the optimizer just constructed. Conversely any finite pair satisfying the two constraints gives a stationary point, hence the unique maximum: concavity gives the tangent inequality for the objective, and its linear term vanishes along the feasible affine space. Finally, the logistic map is one-to-one; two parameter pairs yielding the same \(t_i^*\) at two distinct sites have equal intercept and slope. This proves existence and uniqueness of the exact solution to the two moment equations.

If \(k=a_0\), the row mean equation at the smallest possible target gives \(\sum_i (i-a_0)p_i(1-t_i)=0\). Each summand is nonnegative, so \(t_i=1\) at every \(i>a_0\). The mass equation forces the displayed value of \(t_{a_0}\). There is already a feasible vector, so the forced value lies in \([0,1]\); explicitly its numerator equals \(\sum_{i>a_0}(i-a_0-1)p_i\ge0\), and \(\theta<1\) makes it less than \(p_{a_0}\). If \(k+1=b_0\), the analogous largest-target row forces \(t_i=0\) at every \(i<b_0\), and its mass equation gives \(t_{b_0}=\theta/p_{b_0}\). It is positive, and it is at most one because \(\theta=\sum_i(i-b_0+1)p_i\le p_{b_0}\). When both boundary cases apply there are two source sites, \(\theta=p_{b_0}\), and the formulas coincide with the diagonal channel. These arguments give all nonintegral boundary cases and show that their entire adjacent-target feasible set is a singleton.

Now let \(\phi\) be convex. Its interpolation \(\bar\phi\) is convex, and a supporting affine function \(\ell\) at \(\mu\) exists. For an interior point one may choose any slope between its left and right slopes; for an endpoint of a nontrivial interval use the endpoint slope; the one-site case was specified separately. For any feasible target law,

\[
\sum_jq_j\phi_j-\bar\phi(\mu)
=\sum_jq_j[\phi_j-\ell(j)]\ge0,
\]

because \(\sum_jq_j\ell(j)=\ell(\mu)=\bar\phi(\mu)\). Every summand is nonnegative, so equality holds exactly when \(q\) is supported on the contact sites of \(\ell\). This proves the full-face characterization. If \(\mu\) is integral, the constant target attains equality. Otherwise, the adjacent target has expectation \((1-\theta)\phi_k+\theta\phi_{k+1}=\bar\phi(\mu)\), so \(r^*\) attains equality. The source term \(\sum_i p_i\phi_i\) is fixed; consequently \(G_\phi\) is constant on this entire minimum-potential face. Global uniqueness of the information minimizer then proves uniqueness of its minimum \(G_\phi+I\) on that face. Convexity also gives \(G_\phi(r)\ge0\) for any feasible array, by applying the convex interpolation to each posterior source law and using its row mean, although this sign alone does not give the scalar budget.

Suppose \(p\) is log-concave. In the interior logistic case the nonzero posterior laws obey

\[
\begin{aligned}
\log s_k(i)&=\log p_i-\log(1+e^{\lambda+\eta i})-\log(1-\theta),\\
\log s_{k+1}(i)&=\log p_i+\lambda+\eta i-\log(1+e^{\lambda+\eta i})-\log\theta.
\end{aligned}
\]

The sequence \(\log p_i\) is concave. The real function \(x\mapsto\log(1+e^{\lambda+\eta x})\) is convex, since its second derivative is \(\eta^2 e^{\lambda+\eta x}/(1+e^{\lambda+\eta x})^2\ge0\). Therefore both displayed sequences are concave. Their support is all of \(D\), which proves the claimed log-concavity there and for their zero extensions.

At the lower boundary, the lower posterior is a point mass at \(a_0\). The upper posterior is proportional to \(p\), except that its first entry is multiplied by \(t_{a_0}^*\in[0,1]\). Reducing an endpoint entry preserves every log-concavity inequality: the only affected interior inequality has that entry on its right-hand side, which can only decrease. If the factor is zero, the remaining positive support is the shorter interval. At the upper boundary the same argument applies with the last entry of the lower posterior multiplied by \(1-t_{b_0}^*\), while the upper posterior is a point mass. In the integral-mean case the sole posterior is \(p\) itself. Thus all cases have the stated posterior log-concavity and interval support.

For the product assertion, the product array has the required source marginal. At every positive target its posterior is a product of the one-dimensional posteriors, each with its required mean. Hence it satisfies all vector row mean equations. Entropy of a finite product law is the sum of the factor entropies, by direct expansion of its logarithm, so its mutual information is \(\sum_v I(r^{*,[v]})\).

Conversely, take any vector feasible array. The marginal pair \((J_v,X_v)\) is a one-dimensional feasible pair: the tower property gives \(\mathbb E[X_v\mid J_v]=\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X_v\mid\mathbf J]\mid J_v]=J_v\). Since the source coordinates are independent, the chain rule and the fact that further conditioning cannot increase conditional entropy give

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{MI}(\mathbf X;\mathbf J)
&=\sum_v S(p^{[v]})-\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbf X\mid\mathbf J)\\
&\ge\sum_v\left[S(p^{[v]})-\operatorname{Ent}(X_v\mid J_v)\right]\\
&=\sum_v\operatorname{MI}(X_v;J_v)
\ge\sum_v I(r^{*,[v]}).
\end{aligned}
\]

For clarity, the conditional entropy step follows by expanding \(\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbf X\mid\mathbf J)\) as \(\sum_v\operatorname{Ent}(X_v\mid X_1,\ldots,X_{v-1},\mathbf J)\), and comparing each summand with \(\operatorname{Ent}(X_v\mid J_v)\); the difference is a conditional mutual information and is nonnegative. This proves the full product information minimum.

For a separable convex potential, each one-dimensional feasible marginal has expected target potential at least \(\bar\phi^{[v]}(\mu_v)\). Summing proves the asserted lower bound, and the product array attains it. On the minimum-potential face the total drop is the fixed number \(\sum_v[\sum_i p^{[v]}_i\phi^{[v]}_i-\bar\phi^{[v]}(\mu_v)]\). Adding the established minimum of mutual information proves the exact additive formula for the minimum budget on that face.

Finally specialize to the square law. Its potential satisfies \(\phi_i=\tfrac12(\log p_{\max}-\log p_i)\). Hence, for nonintegral \(\mu\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
G_\phi(r^*)&=\frac12\left[S(p)+(1-\theta)\log p_k+\theta\log p_{k+1}\right],\\
I(r^*)&=\mathsf h(\theta)-\sum_i p_i\mathsf h(t_i^*).
\end{aligned}
\]

For integral \(\mu\) the same computation at its constant target gives \(G_\phi(r^*)=\tfrac12[S(p)+\log p_\mu]\) and \(I(r^*)=0\). Log-concavity of \(w\) makes \(\phi\) convex and \(p\) log-concave, so all the preceding results apply. Since \(G_\phi\) is fixed on the minimum-potential face and \(r^*\) is its information minimizer, the existence of any array on that face with budget at most \(\log2\) is equivalent to the corresponding displayed scalar inequality. For product weights the square source factorizes and the original potential is separable, so the product formula gives exactly the asserted conditional tensorization.

These computations do not establish either remaining scalar inequality. In particular, log-concavity of the posterior source sequences alone has not provided a geometric construction in actual continuous fibers, nor an estimate comparing every halfspace's original mixed-integer volume with the square-law information budget. Thus no actual-depth conclusion is used or claimed.
statement:
All logarithms are natural. Let \(D=\{a_0,a_0+1,\ldots,b_0\}\) be a nonempty finite integer interval, and let \(p_i>0\) for \(i\in D\), with \(\sum_Dp_i=1\). Both array indices range over \(D\). Define the canonical objects

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal F(p)&=\left\{r\ge0:\ \sum_jr_{j,i}=p_i\ (i\in D),\quad
  \sum_i r_{j,i}(i-j)=0\ (j\in D)\right\},\\
q_j&=\sum_i r_{j,i},\qquad S(v)=-\sum_xv_x\log v_x,\\
H(r)&=-\sum_{j,i}r_{j,i}\log\frac{r_{j,i}}{p_i},\qquad
I(r)=S(q)-H(r).
\end{aligned}
\]

Zero summands are interpreted by continuity. Thus, for a pair \((J,X)\) with law \(r\), feasibility means that \(X\) has law \(p\) and \(\mathbb E[X\mid J]=J\), while \(H(r)=\operatorname{Ent}(J\mid X)\) and \(I(r)=\operatorname{MI}(X;J)\). Here \(\operatorname{Ent}\) denotes Shannon entropy or conditional Shannon entropy, and \(\operatorname{MI}\) denotes mutual information. Set \(\mu=\sum_iip_i\).

There is a unique minimizer \(r^*\) of \(I\) over the entire \(\mathcal F(p)\). If \(\mu\) is integral, it is the constant-target array \(r^*_{\mu,i}=p_i\), with every other row zero; its information is zero. This includes the one-site interval.

Suppose \(\mu\notin\mathbb Z\), and put \(k=\lfloor\mu\rfloor\) and \(\theta=\mu-k\in(0,1)\). The minimizer has target law \(q^*_k=1-\theta\), \(q^*_{k+1}=\theta\), with all other target probabilities zero. Write

\[
r^*_{k+1,i}=p_i t_i^*,\qquad r^*_{k,i}=p_i(1-t_i^*).
\]

The vector \(t^*\) is the unique maximizer of \(\sum_i p_i\mathsf h(t_i)\) subject to

\[
0\le t_i\le1,\qquad
\sum_i p_it_i=\theta,\qquad
\sum_i ip_it_i=(k+1)\theta,
\qquad
\mathsf h(t)=-t\log t-(1-t)\log(1-t).
\]

If \(a_0<k\) and \(k+1<b_0\), there is a unique pair \((\lambda,\eta)\in\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\) satisfying these two moment equations with

\[
t_i^*=\frac{\exp(\lambda+\eta i)}{1+\exp(\lambda+\eta i)}.
\]

These equations, with the specified unique real solution, define the channel exactly and do not refer to a numerical optimizer. The boundary formulas are as follows:

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
k=a_0:
&t_i^*=1\ (i>a_0),\qquad
t_{a_0}^*=\dfrac{\theta-(1-p_{a_0})}{p_{a_0}},\\[6pt]
k+1=b_0:
&t_i^*=0\ (i<b_0),\qquad
t_{b_0}^*=\dfrac{\theta}{p_{b_0}}.
\end{array}
\]

Both formulas apply consistently on a two-site interval, where \(t_{a_0}^*=0\) and \(t_{b_0}^*=1\). All displayed boundary probabilities belong to \([0,1]\).

Here is an explicit feasible channel needed for the reduction and existence assertions. For any finitely supported integer-valued probability law with mean \(k+\theta\), put

\[
\begin{aligned}
a&=\Pr(X\le k),& b&=\Pr(X\ge k+1),\\
u&=\mathbb E[k-X\mid X\le k],&
v&=\mathbb E[X-k-1\mid X\ge k+1],&
L&=1+u+v.
\end{aligned}
\]

Then \(a,b>0\), and the assignment probabilities

\[
\Pr(J=k+1\mid X=i)=
\begin{cases}
\theta v/(aL),&i\le k,\\
\theta(1+u)/(bL),&i\ge k+1
\end{cases}
\]

define a feasible array with the adjacent target law above. This channel need not equal \(t^*\). Applied to the target law of any \(r\in\mathcal F(p)\), it gives a postprocessing \(J\mapsto K\) such that \(\mathbb E[J\mid K]=K\), \(K\in\{k,k+1\}\), and \(\operatorname{MI}(X;K)\le\operatorname{MI}(X;J)\). If equality holds, then \(J=K\) almost surely.

Let \(\phi_i\) be any real convex sequence on \(D\), meaning that its successive differences are nondecreasing. Let \(\bar\phi\) be its piecewise-linear convex interpolation on \([a_0,b_0]\), and define the original-potential drop

\[
G_\phi(r)=\sum_{j,i}r_{j,i}(\phi_i-\phi_j).
\]

The minimum expected target potential over \(\mathcal F(p)\) is \(\bar\phi(\mu)\), and \(r^*\) attains it. More precisely, for any affine function \(\ell\) supporting \(\bar\phi\) at \(\mu\), the complete minimum-potential face is

\[
\left\{r\in\mathcal F(p):q_j=0\text{ whenever }\phi_j>\ell(j)\right\}.
\]

On a one-site interval take \(\ell\) to have the specified value at that site. Thus \(r^*\) simultaneously minimizes mutual information and every convex target potential, although a convex potential can have other minimizing arrays. Among all its minimum-potential arrays, \(r^*\) is the unique minimizer of \(G_\phi+I\).

If \(p\) is log-concave, meaning \(p_i^2\ge p_{i-1}p_{i+1}\) at every interior site, each nonzero posterior source law \(s_j(i)=r^*_{j,i}/q^*_j\), extended by zero outside its support, is log-concave and has interval support.

For an independent product of \(n\) such source laws \(p^{[v]}\) on intervals \(D_v\), let \(p_{\mathbf i}=\prod_{v=1}^np^{[v]}_{i_v}\), and use the canonical vector barycentric equations \(\mathbb E[\mathbf X\mid\mathbf J]=\mathbf J\). The product array \(r^{\mathrm{prod}}_{\mathbf j,\mathbf i}=\prod_{v=1}^n r^{*,[v]}_{j_v,i_v}\) minimizes \(I\) over all vector feasible arrays, with

\[
\min_{r\in\mathcal F(p)}I(r)=\sum_{v=1}^n I(r^{*,[v]}).
\]

For any separable convex potential \(\phi_{\mathbf i}=\sum_{v=1}^n\phi^{[v]}_{i_v}\), it also attains the minimum expected target potential \(\sum_v\bar\phi^{[v]}(\mu_v)\). On that entire minimum-potential face the minimum value of \(G_\phi+I\) is exactly

\[
\sum_{v=1}^n\left(G_{\phi^{[v]}}(r^{*,[v]})+I(r^{*,[v]})\right).
\]

No uniqueness assertion for all vector minimizers is needed here.

In particular, take positive log-concave weights \(w_i\), put \(w_{\max}=\max_{i\in D}w_i\), retain \(\phi_i=\log(w_{\max}/w_i)\), and sample from \(p_i=w_i^2/\sum_jw_j^2\). Write \(p_{\max}=\max_{i\in D}p_i\). The potential associated directly with this source law is \(2\phi\); throughout this statement \(G_\phi\) uses the original \(\phi\). If \(\mu\notin\mathbb Z\), the original square-law selector question is equivalent to the following explicit inequality at the uniquely defined channel above:

\[
\frac12\left[S(p)+(1-\theta)\log p_k+\theta\log p_{k+1}\right]
+\mathsf h(\theta)-\sum_i p_i\mathsf h(t_i^*)\ \le\ \log2.
\tag{*}
\]

If \(\mu\in\mathbb Z\), its equivalent inequality is \(\tfrac12[S(p)+\log p_\mu]\le\log2\). A strict failure of the appropriate inequality excludes every minimum-potential array, not just the adjacent-target array. A proof for every one-dimensional positive log-concave law would imply the budget \(n\log2\) for independent product weights. Neither of these scalar inequalities is asserted here. None of the structural conclusions alone supplies a lower bound on actual mixed-integer halfspace depth.
